stories.title: US to get 'permanent control' over Greenland security
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has said that he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington "permanent control" over Greenland's security that would bar Russia and China from setting up bases in the Arctic territory. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Mr Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance. Denmark and Greenland - an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen - both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week. But the terms of the deal remain uncertain, and Denmark maintains that its sovereignty remains intact. In a statement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the deal as "an agreement which at the same time recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination". "I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Mr Trump said on his Truth Social network.

stories.title: Government should prioritise diversifying tax base - IMF
stories.summary: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva has called on the Irish Government to prioritise diversifying the country's tax base. "It is very important for Ireland to diversify the tax base. This world of uncertainty we have entered, it's not going to disappear. "So having a sound foundation for public finances means, among other things, diversifying your revenues. And you have space to do it," she said. Ms Georgieva added: "Let's remember one thing ... the crisis, when it happened, it was incredibly painful and it led to a recognition that the soundness of public finances is a protection for people and businesses. Keep on that lesson." The IMF managing director said the Government was able to "cushion the country" from economic shocks but also called on them to avoid providing support to people who do not need it. "You are so fortunate to have strong fiscal position. Your debt levels are low, you have surplus in your budget.

stories.title: Minister accused of protected disclosure 'incompetence'
stories.summary: Labour TD Alan Kelly has accused Minister Helen McEntee of either "incompetence or a mistake" in her handling of a protected disclosure, adding that it is something that will "haunt" her and the Government in which she served. Speaking during Leaders' Questions in the Dáil, Deputy Kelly accused Ms McEntee - when she was Minister for Justice - of having "acted without legal authority" by having "revealed Brian O'Reilly's identity, thereby depriving him of the legal protections he was entitled to and exposing the nature of his allegations". Deputy Kelly was taking issue with the minister's decision to direct that the investigation of Brian O'Reilly's protected disclosure "be removed from your Secretary General and be redirected to An Garda Siochána, thereby usurping the OPDC statutory direction, which is their role". He said that the minister had "directly interfered with a serious and significant protective disclosure" and brought about consequences that were "detrimental to Brian O'Reilly's life, his career, his livelihood and well-being of him, his wife, his children, his family". The Labour TD said that he did not believe she had acted deliberately, and so must have acted out of "incompetence or a mistake". Minister McEntee, who was taking Leaders' Questions, rejected the deputy's claims.

stories.title: Lagarde say ECB to decide 'meeting by meeting' on rates
stories.summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said today that any further interest rate increases by the ECB "will depend on the future." The ECB has decided to "actually assess the situation, look at the data, look at three things - the inflation outlook, the underlying inflation, and the transmission of our monetary policy into the economy," she said. "And it's on the basis of these three elements and on the data that we receive, the projections that we produce, that we then decide what we have to do," she added. She said the "only thing that we are absolutely confident about is the goal. We have to bring inflation to 2% and we have to offer price stability to Europeans," she explained. She said the ECB would decide "meeting by meeting" what is appropriate, whether that is to hold, increase, or cut interest rates, although cutting rates "is very unlikely at the moment," she added. Mortgage payers are "absolutely" in the mind of ECB decisionmakers when considering changes to interest rates, she added.

stories.title: Diana's brother insists he's 'telling truth' about King
stories.summary: The brother of Britain's Princess Diana has insisted that he is "telling the truth" about his conversation with King Charles after Diana's death, describing the alleged comments as "monstrous". A dispute erupted between King Charles and Charles Spencer, who claimed the then-prince told him, "rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough", days after Diana's death in 1997. The claims are made in a new memoir by Mr Spencer, chronicling his late sister. In the latest extract from the memoir serialised in the Daily Mail, he further claimed that the then Prince Charles sounded "giddily elated - like a lottery winner" when he rang him following Diana's death. In an extract of an interview with the BBC, Mr Spencer said that the claims prompted an "unprecedented" response from Buckingham Palace who said "the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason". He questioned whether the official response showed the King was actually embarrassed.

stories.title: Dunne doubts there's appetite for more GAA rule changes
stories.summary: Former Offaly forward Nigel Dunne has questioned whether there is a sufficient appetite amongst the GAA public for further rule changes in Gaelic football. Several tweaks will be trialled over the coming months in third level Ryan Cup fixtures, following research and discussion amongst members of the Expert Advisory Group, which is chaired by former Mayo player and manager Kevin McStay. The EAG - which was formed following the work of the Football Review Committee - is charged with monitoring trends in the game and has come up with a number of proposals to be introduced in the coming months. Among the key proposals is the banning of fisted points (unless the ball is already in flight), limiting the number of consecutive handpasses to three and awarding four points for a goal. A backcourt rule, whereby the ball cannot return back over the halfway line, and a modified kickout rule, where the ball is no longer required to travel beyond the two-point arc, are also included in the slate of changes. "In isolation they're fine and I don’t disagree with them but the problem is why change now?

stories.title: Derry edge cagey affair with Galway to move into fourth
stories.summary: Derry City moved into fourth spot following a hard-fought win over Galway United at the Ryan McBride Brandywell Stadium. Adam O'Reilly's close-range goal just before the break was enough for the Candystripes and with Dundalk losing to Shelbourne, they move into fourth place, with four league games remaining. The home side went close on 10 minutes but O'Reilly's 20 yard drive, which had United goalkeeper Hugo Pires Da Cunha beaten, flew over the bar. Just after the mid-way point of the half, the visitors created their first opening when Stephen Walsh found space inside the box and just as he was about to pull the trigger, Cameron Dummigan came sliding across to divert the ball away for a corner. Minutes before the interval Walsh went close again, this time his overhead kick from 10 yards was straight at City keeper Tom Norcott. Right on the stroke of half-time a lovely passing move ended Brandon Fleming finding Michael Duffy and his left wing cut-back found O'Reilly, who turned the ball home from close range, despite Da Cunha's best attempts at trying to keep it out.

stories.title: Nankivell: ' I would love to stay here at Munster'
stories.summary: Munster centre Alex Nankivell has confessed his wishes to remain in Ireland and with the province for the foreseeable, as he heads into his fourth season at the club, and a contract year. The former Chiefs back joined up with the province in Autumn of 2023, and has been a shining light since his arrival, culminating in winning Munster player of the year for the 2025/26 season. Now 29, Nankivell has thoroughly enjoyed his time in Ireland and would be keen to stay on, and potentially line out in green. "I would love to stay here at Munster", he told reporters on Wednesday. "It is definitely in the back of my mind, particularly coming off contract after this season. "I guess the thing about if I re-sign, international rugby is the pinnacle, in my opinion. I've had dreams to play for the All Blacks, and I didn't really think about it when I came over as I didn't think the opportunity would present itself to become Irish-qualified being here, but now it kind of does.

stories.title: New Irish Writing: The Most Normal Woman by Roisín Kiberd
stories.summary: We present an extract from The Most Normal Woman, the new essay collection by Roisin Kiberd. In her new collection of essays, Roisin Kiberd explores the many ways we change ourselves in pursuit of perfection – or simply normality – and the toll it takes on our inner lives. Weaving critical commentary with personal experience, she explores Botox, blondeness, exercise addiction, and subcultures including the underground drag scene and competitive dog shows to better understand how beauty is judged and defined. In 2017, on something of a whim, I found myself in Hong Kong, staying at a flat down the street from the Night Market. One evening I set out, past shops with cats in the windows, restaurants selling family-size hot pots and their stranger, smaller cousin, the hot pot for one, past cafes inexplicably dedicated to perfecting the art of making toast, to a tunnel-shaped street lit with neon, hoardings over everything, sunglasses and belts and shoes and wallets and, of course, handbags, sprawled out on displays, with rapid-talking vendors shouting over each other. I'm the type to find the automated cash registers at Tesco overwhelming; the Night Market in Hong Kong was sensory overload, pulling me in, as though the only way out was to locate the replica handbag I was looking for. I’d seen it mostly on Instagram, on the arm of a paranormally long-legged blonde woman I followed who lived in LA. The Givenchy Antigona is still in production now, a black leather tote with short handles and a weird, angular flap on top that doesn’t actually open. Like a lot of Riccardo Tisci-era Givenchy (his reign began in 2005, and ended in 2017) it has a severe, Catholic look to it that I now associate with mid-career Kanye. I walked past rows of bags, some of them dreadful, some of them accurate, some of them decoys for much more accurate bags, hidden upstairs in the buildings behind the stalls. After a while a combination of tiredness and hunger set in –I’d been living on SkyFlakes crackers and canned iced coffee for much of this trip – and I told myself I’d found a good enough vendor. I got talking to an extremely enthusiastic young woman, who led me into a corridor behind the stall and presented me with a catalogue of bags.

stories.summary: Duncan Sheik, the Grammy-nominated Barely Breathing singer and Grammy and Tony-winning Spring Awakening composer, has died aged 56. Best known for his 1996 song Barely Breathing as well as for writing the music for the coming-of-age musical Spring Awakening, Sheik died on Thursday night "surrounded by love", according to a statement shared on his Instagram account. The US musician was receiving medical care and was described as being in a "critical but stable condition" hours before his death. The statement, posted on Friday, said: "The world has a lost a singular talent, and deeply influential voice in music and theatre. "From his Grammy-nominated hit Barely Breathing to his groundbreaking, Tony and Grammy Award-winning work on Spring Awakening, Duncan's artistry touched many and leaves an indelible mark on the cultural landscape. He was remembered for his "sensitivity, wit, intelligence, and depth of spirit he brought to those who knew and loved him".

stories.title: OMMA founder on building a 'secret forest' cafe in wartorn Kyiv
stories.summary: Nastya Kharytonova, the Dublin-based Ukrainian founder of OMMA matcha café, speaks to Charlotte Ryan from Kyiv about endurance and inspiration, as she prepares to open the second branch of her business in the Ukrainian capital. The night after I spoke with Kharytonova about her plans to open a Kyiv branch of the café, the warehouse that had built all the dreamy, ethereal and highly specific furniture for the project was destroyed in an air attack. It was a close call for the team, as they had already moved the furniture from the warehouse, but one of many. In the weeks leading up to the launch of OMMA's new space in collaboration with Ukrainian loungewear brand LONDI, the facade of a building 200 metres from their new office was destroyed by a drone. Kharytonova recalls being in the city centre as it happened, seeing the drone "above my head, and then you hear the explosion the second after". OMMA's new opening coincided with a change of tactics by the Russian army over the end of the summer, as it increased daytime assaults, on top of continuing to batter Ukrainian cities at night.

stories.summary: Google's Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities. It's the first known instance ⁠of the company's AI systems autonomously committing such an act. The hacks occurred in May during a cybersecurity test carried out by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations. During a standard testing evaluation, Gemini models found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites they thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said in a statement. "We ensured the three entities were made ‌aware, and we worked with ⁠our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes," Ms Adkins said. "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly," she added.

stories.title: Man charged in Michael Healy-Rae assault investigation
stories.summary: A man in his 50s has been charged in relation to the investigation into an assault on Kerry TD Michael Healy-Rae in Dublin on Wednesday afternoon. He is due to appear before a sitting of Dublin District Court at the Criminal Courts of Justice today at 10.30am. Mr Healy-Rae was travelling in his own vehicle on Cork Street in Dublin city at around 4.10pm on Wednesday when he was approached by a man who assaulted him through the window of his car. Following the assault, the Kerry TD was taken from the road by gardaí who were quickly on the scene. They took him to Kevin Street Garda Station and an ambulance was called. He attended St Vincent's University Hospital for his injuries, and was discharged around 9pm on Wednesday night, having needed stitches for injuries to his face and mouth.

stories.title: Europe's AI firms challenge US calls for slowdown
stories.summary: Europe's leading AI company Mistral and others have accused US rivals of using safety concerns to entrench their dominance, rejecting Anthropic's calls for advanced developers to slow down as Europe struggles to catch up. Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei in an online essay urged firms to slow the pace at which they improve AI model capabilities and called for an antitrust waiver allowing leading developers to jointly develop safety measures after researchers warned about the dangers of AI, including that it could wipe out humanity. While OpenAI's chief Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk also warned about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems and agreed on the need to pace development, companies and officials in Europe have taken a more sceptical line. "Some incumbents are using this moment to consolidate their market position, pushing for regulation designed to favour them over competitors," said French startup Mistral in a statement, noting that the risks had already been clear for months. Europe has produced few frontier AI developers, with 3-year-old Mistral seen as the region's best hope for developing its own frontier AI model to challenge US and Chinese dominance. For now, the region relies heavily on models developed by OpenAI, Anthropic or Microsoft, leaving many wary of the ongoing dependence on US tech.

stories.title: Council of Europe body slams 'fake' Russia vote
stories.summary: Russia is staging a "fake election that will produce a fake parliament", a group of European politicians and exiled Russian activists at Europe's leading human rights watchdog have said. Russians are voting (from today until Sunday) in a tightly controlled election expected to see President Vladimir Putin tighten his grip on power even further after 26 years in power. It is the country's first parliamentary election since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. The polls are "fake 'elections' that will produce a fake parliament," said the Platform for Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. "The incoming State Duma must not be recognised as democratically elected or as the legitimate representative of the Russian people." The dialogue platform comprises European politicians and exiled Russian opposition politicians including Vladimir Kara-Murza and Mikhail Khodorkovsky and respected rights campaigner Oleg Orlov.

stories.title: NFL Preview: Are the Chiefs running back to play-offs?
stories.summary:
Last season's failure to make the play-offs left Kansas City and, in particular, their offence open to real criticism for the first time in the Patrick Mahomes era. After week 1, though, the arrival of one player may have quelled those queries for another year. By signing Kenneth Walker in free agency, the Chiefs not only got the Super Bowl MVP but also a star who could give them their first 1,000-yard running back in nearly ten years. In only his first game, the former Michigan State man ran for over 170 yards and scored two touchdowns. For context, it had been 694 days since the Chiefs ran for over 170 yards in a game as a team. Not a bad first day of work. It's very rare you get the chance to sign one of the top players from a championship-winning team in any sport. The closest comparison might be Leicester City's Premier League triumph: they managed to hold on to Jamie Vardy and Riyad Mahrez but lost N’Golo Kante. Like Kante, Walker could be described as the engine room of the Seahawks team that won it all last season.

Walker leaving the Super Bowl champions and heading to Missouri caused quite a stir. But because of his position, it was almost expected that when he lifted the Lombardi back in February, that would be the last time we would see him in navy and neon. In 2025, the average salary of running backs was the third-lowest of any position in the NFL, meaning they earned less on average than kickers. Even though quarterbacks are the only players who touch the ball more often, running backs are not paid anything close to their ball-throwing compatriots.
stories.rssSummary: By signing Kenneth Walker the Kansas City Chiefs are going against the approach that has brought them so much success, but the fact they could sign the Super Bowl MVP speaks volumes for how the position is valued in the NFL.

stories.title: Gleeson calls time on Waterford career at the age of 31
stories.summary: Waterford's Austin Gleeson has announced his retirement from inter-county hurling, bringing an end to a Déise senior career that began in 2014. Gleeson, now 31, was part of the Waterford side that contested the 2017 and 2020 All-Ireland finals, this after he was named both Hurler of the Year and Young Hurler of the Year in 2016. A year previous, the Mount Sion clubman collected senior silverware after his county got the better of Cork in the Division 1 league final. There was also All-Ireland success, with a minor medal won in 2013 and an Under-21 victory three years later. After opting out of the Waterford set-up in 2024, Gleeson returned and was part of the squad during Peter Queally's two years at the helm, though he did not see any championship action, with injuries curtailing the forward's involvement. Gleeson's decision, perhaps, is not surprising, given the signals he was getting earlier this year. Speaking on Off The Ball, he said: "I'm done now. I knew it at the start of 2026. There was one training session I remember in particular where it didn't go the best. It was 23 December; we trained down in Passage.

stories.title: Ronaldo in Portugal squad, despite retirement speculation
stories.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has been included in new Portugal manager Jorge Jesus' first 25-man squad for the defending champions' upcoming four Nations League matches. In August, Ronaldo fuelled speculation about his retirement plans after saying the coming year would probably be the last of his playing career. The 41-year-old Portugal captain is one of the most decorated players in soccer history, having won major trophies with Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and current club Al-Nassr since making his senior debut for Sporting in 2002. Ronaldo, a five-time Ballon d'Or winner, was unable to add a World Cup title to his list of honours after Portugal were knocked out in the last 16 by eventual champions Spain, leaving the sport's biggest prize absent from his trophy cabinet. Ronaldo confirmed in July that the 2026 World Cup would be his last, but he was unwilling to make a hasty call on his international future. "His performance is what matters. The past doesn't count," Jorge Jesus told a press conference.

stories.title: Jackman: 'URC should be the bare minimum' for Leinster
stories.summary: Former Leinster and Ireland hooker Bernard Jackman has claimed that defending their URC title should be the minimum target for Leinster this season. Leo Cullen's men defeated the Vodacom Bulls in the final of each last two editions, having missed out on the first three titles in the revamped league. "(Leinster) don't like people saying this, but the URC should be the bare minimum when they have that much budget and that many international players, that many British and Irish Lions", Jackman said. "Unfortunately, with the squad they have and looking at how strong French rugby is, that Bordeaux game, and I know every other final or semi-final Leinster have been really close, but that Bordeaux game was a real gulf in class on the day. "They're not getting any weaker. I don't know if you've been following up, but the French clubs are so aggressive recruiting for next year already, trying to buy lads out of contracts in the Premiership. They are just driven. "The whole machine there is absolutely well-oiled and vibrant. So, yeah, to win Europe looks like it's further away than ever. But having said that, (if) Leinster put their best team out, they're a match for anybody."

stories.title: Four new Irish hotels awarded Michelin Keys in 2026 awards
stories.summary: Three Irish hotels have been newly awarded Michelin Keys in the Guide's 2026 awards. While the renowned Michelin Star recognises the most outstanding restaurants in the world, the Michelin Key does the same for outstanding hotels. There are three levels of the distinction: one key, two keys and three keys, with three being the top award, much like the Michelin Stars. Created in April 2024, the award aims to find the crème de la crème of hotels, highlighting those that excel in design, architecture, service and personality. This year's awards awarded almost 500 new hotels with keys, and more than 80 with upgrades. With more than 9,000 hotels now awarded with keys, the Michelin Keys rank excellence in terms of five criteria: architecture and interior design; personality and character of the hotel; quality and consistency of service; value offered between experience and the price paid; and how the hotel contributes to its locality. The Leinster in Co Dublin, the Fitzwilliam Hotel in Co Dublin, Glenlo Abbey Hotel in Co Galway and Marlfield House Hotel in Co Wexford each received One Key distinctions, bringing the number of Irish hotels with Michelin Keys to 20. Two hotels retained their Three Key distinction in this year's list: Adare Manor, Co Limerick and Ballyfin Demesne, Co Laois.

stories.title: EU-Canada: Marriage of convenience or red rag to Trump?
stories.summary: Ursula von der Leyen's startling offer for Canada to become "the first associate member" of the EU during Wednesday’s State of the Union speech took many by surprise, not least the member states whose approval would be required for such an outcome. "First we’d heard of it," remarked one EU diplomat. "It was a surprise," said a second diplomat, "but not a negative surprise." stories.title: Inquest hears scans failed to identify neurological issue
stories.summary: A verdict of medical misadventure has been recorded in the death of a mother of three young children who had suffered severe headaches for several weeks but was told by doctors that scans had failed to identify any neurological problem. However, one consultant who subsequently reviewed two scans on the patient told an inquest that they showed signs of cerebral oedema (swelling of the brain). Stacie Bailey, aged 33, a married mother of three from Whitefield Manor, Bettystown, Co Meath, died at Beaumont Hospital in Dublin on 23 November 2023 shortly after undergoing emergency surgery to drain fluid from her brain. The civil servant, who was originally from Skerries, Co Dublin, was the subject of an urgent transfer to Beaumont from Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital, Drogheda, Co Louth where she had collapsed and suffered a cardiac arrest. The inquest heard Ms Bailey had attended the hospital's emergency department four times in the space of a fortnight shortly before her death. Ms Bailey’s mother, Julie Radford, who formally identified her daughter’s body to gardaí, told the hearing how Stacie had complained that she felt "like her head was being crushed".

stories.summary: Sinn Féin leader Mary-Lou McDonald has expressed shock at the attack on Michael Healy-Rae, adding that the incident should be a "wake-up call". Mr Healy-Rae was travelling in his own vehicle on Cork Street in Dublin city at around 4.10pm on Wednesday when he was approached by a man who assaulted him through the window of his car. Speaking to reporters in Belfast, Ms McDonald said she wished Mr Healy-Rae "only the best" and that there must be "zero tolerance to that type of behaviour". "I think people in public life have to at all times be cognisant of their safety. Having said that, for the most part, people are respectful and decent. "Those that carry out an attack like this are in the very, very tiny minority but they are amongst us," she said. "We have to be able to move freely in our communities and to go about our work.

stories.title: Buffett steps down as Berkshire chairman, son succeeds
stories.summary: Berkshire Hathaway said today that Warren Buffett will step down as chairman and become chairman emeritus, effective immediately, nine months after handing the CEO reins to longtime lieutenant Greg Abel. The company named his son, Howard Buffett, a director since 1993, as chairman. Warren Buffett is credited with transforming Berkshire from a failing textile company into a $1.1 trillion conglomerate while building an investment philosophy that influenced generations of investors and executives, making him one of the most consequential figures in modern corporate America. Berkshire's Class B shares were last down 0.3% in premarket trading. Buffett's reputation has also been reflected in the company's valuation, with investors for years ascribing a "Buffett premium" to its shares. The conglomerate's price-to-book value has fallen since Buffett announced he would step down as CEO, slipping from around $1.62 to $1.53, according to data compiled by LSEG. Berkshire remains the only financial firm in the trillion-dollar market-value club dominated by technology giants.

stories.title: UN holds third informal poll for new chief United Nations
stories.summary: The UN's most powerful body, the Security Council, met today to again gauge the popularity of contenders to lead the organization as world leaders prepare to gather for its annual signature event. No results have yet emerged from the secret indicative vote which took more than one hour, with France's envoy to the UN and the Council's rotating President Jerome Bonnafont saying only "the third round of straw polls has taken place." No frontrunner emerged from the first two rounds of informal polls with eight candidates now vying to follow Secretary-General Antonio Guterres when his term concludes at the end of December. Several council members have declared their desire for the embattled UN to have its first woman leader. Guyanese ex-foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett narrowly led the second round of the secret process, while Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan came in second and Argentina's Rafael Grossi, the current head of the UN nuclear watchdog, was third. Other candidates include Macky Sall of Senegal, Ecuador's Ivonne A-Baki, Chile's Michelle Bachelet, Ecuador's Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Uganda's Olara Otunnu.

stories.title: Pat's aiming to keep foot firmly on the pedal in Sligo
stories.summary: St Pat's Athletic will be looking to regain top spot in the Premier Division when they travel to basement club Sligo Rovers on Saturday evening. After Shamrock Rovers and Bohemians both secured dramatic wins in an intruiging title race, Pat's will be looking to keep up their end of the bargain and maintain their recent good run. Recent wins over the Hoops at Richmond Park and then a thumping of Dundalk at Oriel underlined their intent, with Stephen Kenny looking to mastermind a first league title for the club since 2013. For Sligo, after two decades in the top flight, the drop down looks inevitable. Darren Purse's arrival as manager at the end of July has failed to provide a spark so far, though injuries, the arrival of players new to the league and the departure of the industrious Will Fitzgerald have not helped in creating an equilibrium Purse would have liked . Goals have been hard to come by. You have to go back to 22 May for the Bit O' Red's last league victory: a 2-1 victory away to Shamrock Rovers, a win of the smash-and-grab variety. Despite losing to Galway on Monday last, Sligo did show an endeavour that was absent in previous games, with teenagers Aidan Gabbidon and Reuben Gillespie making their first senior starts for the club, while Liam Hughes was making his debut between the posts. Purse was accentuating the positives afterwards, telling reporters: "If the players keep playing like that we'll nick a result whether that’s on Saturday or going forward in the next games after that.
